blocks.text: 1. Similarity Metrics
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161743-860907633.png
Similarity metrics cover how distance between vectors actually gets measured, moving from vector structure to vector comparison.
This topic surveys the mathematical formulas that turn two vectors into a single similarity number.
2. From Nearby Points To A Number
As covered in What are Embeddings, similar meaning means nearby points, but saying two vectors are nearby requires an actual, precise way to measure distance.
This topic surveys the concrete formulas that make that measurement possible.
3. The Three Main Candidates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161743-618897547.png
Cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance are the three most common similarity metrics.
Each gets its own dedicated topic immediately following this one.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","What it measures"],"rows":[["Cosine similarity","The angle between two vectors"],["Dot product","Direction and magnitude combined"],["Euclidean distance","Straight line distance between two points"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Angle Versus Magnitude
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161744-453194405.png
Some metrics care only about a vector's direction, while others also factor in its length.
That distinction is what separates the three main candidates from each other.
5. Normalized Versus Unnormalized Vectors
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161744-204221591.png
Normalizing a vector scales it to a fixed length, leaving only direction.
Once vectors are normalized, several of these metrics become mathematically equivalent.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: On normalized vectors, cosine similarity and dot product produce the exact same ranking of results, since removing magnitude leaves only the angle, which is all cosine similarity ever measured in the first place.

blocks.text: 6. Why Metric Choice Matters
A mismatched metric can rank chunks incorrectly, even with perfectly good embeddings.
The embedding model and the similarity metric need to be paired correctly.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: An embedding model trained and evaluated using cosine similarity can produce noticeably worse rankings if a pipeline instead measures similarity using Euclidean distance, since the model was never optimized for that particular metric.

blocks.text: 7. Computational Cost Across Metrics
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161745-517884108.png
As with the cost of density covered in Dense Embeddings, different metrics carry slightly different computational costs.
That difference matters at the large scale of a real vector database, covered in a later module.
8. Metric Support In Vector Databases
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161745-359296789.png
A vector database, covered in a later module, typically supports only a fixed set of these metrics.
That supported set often constrains which metric a pipeline can actually use.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Which Similarity Metric To Reach For

blocks.alt: Recognizing Which Similarity Metric To Reach For
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161746-975524086.png
Following the embedding model's own recommended metric is usually the safest choice.
Experimenting without model guidance, on the other hand, still benefits from understanding each metric's own tradeoffs, covered next in this module.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using a similarity metric different from the one an embedding model was trained and evaluated with.
Assuming all similarity metrics always produce the same ranking regardless of normalization.
Ignoring which similarity metrics a chosen vector database actually supports before building around one.
Overlooking the small but real computational cost differences between metrics at large scale.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Similarity metrics are the formulas that turn two vectors into a single comparable similarity number.
Cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance are the three most common candidates.
Some metrics care only about direction; others also factor in a vector's magnitude.
Normalizing vectors to a fixed length makes several of these metrics mathematically equivalent.
A mismatched metric can rank chunks incorrectly, even with well trained embeddings.
Different metrics carry slightly different computational costs, which matter at large scale.
Vector databases typically support only a fixed set of metrics, constraining pipeline choices.
Following the embedding model's recommended metric is usually the safest default choice.
Next up: Cosine Similarity, covering the most widely used metric in modern RAG systems in depth.
